title: Nehemiah 13:1–14
context: When the book of Moses is read, the people find the law excluding Ammonites and Moabites from the assembly (Deut 23:3–5) and separate the mixed multitude from Israel. Nehemiah then reports that during his absence Eliashib the priest had given Tobiah a room in the temple courts; on his return he throws out Tobiah’s goods, has the rooms cleansed, restores the Levites’ portions, and appoints faithful treasurers. The Tobiah reform is narrative, and Nehemiah’s prayer “Remember me, my God” (13:14) is shared ground in both traditions.

verses.text: On that day they read in the book of Moses in the hearing of the people; and it was found written in it that an Ammonite and a Moabite should not enter into the assembly of God forever,
verses.arminianNotes:
When the book of Moses was read, “it was found written in it that an Ammonite and a Moabite should not enter into the assembly of God forever.” Arminian readers note that the reading of the law prompts reform, as in chapter 8.

The passage draws on Deuteronomy 23:3–5.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the people responding to what is written.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, and both note that the book of Ruth tells of Ruth the Moabite joining Israel and its God (Ruth 1:16); how these texts relate is discussed.

verses.text: because they didn’t meet the children of Israel with bread and with water, but hired Balaam against them to curse them; however, our God turned the curse into a blessing.
verses.arminianNotes:
The reason given is that they “hired Balaam against them to curse them; however, our God turned the curse into a blessing.” Arminian readers note the reference to Numbers 22–24.

God’s protection of his people is remembered.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see God’s faithfulness in turning a curse into a blessing (Deut 23:5).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the law’s concern is rooted in past hostility to Israel and in God’s protection of his people.

verses.text: It came to pass, when they had heard the law, that they separated all the mixed multitude from Israel.
verses.arminianNotes:
“It came to pass, when they had heard the law, that they separated all the mixed multitude from Israel.” Arminian readers note the people’s response to the law.

The text does not say exactly who was included in “the mixed multitude” or how the separation was carried out.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see obedience to the word as the people understood it.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground, and both read the verse carefully without adding details it does not give.

verses.text: Now before this, Eliashib the priest, who was appointed over the rooms of the house of our God, being allied to Tobiah,
verses.arminianNotes:
“Eliashib the priest, who was appointed over the rooms of the house of our God, being allied to Tobiah.” Arminian readers note the conflict of interest in a priest’s alliance with Nehemiah’s opponent (2:10; 6:17–19).

Whether this Eliashib is the high priest is discussed.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a failure of faithfulness among those entrusted with God’s house.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Tobiah’s connections in Jerusalem were already noted (6:18).

verses.text: had prepared for him a great room, where previously they laid the meal offerings, the frankincense, the vessels, and the tithes of the grain, the new wine, and the oil, which were given by commandment to the Levites, the singers, and the gatekeepers; and the wave offerings for the priests.
verses.arminianNotes:
Eliashib prepared for Tobiah “a great room, where previously they laid the meal offerings, the frankincense, the vessels, and the tithes.” Arminian readers note that space meant for offerings is given to a private ally.

The Levites, singers, and gatekeepers depended on those stores.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the misuse of what belonged to God’s service.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the room had served the support of worship and was turned to another use.

verses.text: But in all this, I was not at Jerusalem; for in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes king of Babylon I went to the king; and after some days I asked leave of the king,
verses.arminianNotes:
“But in all this, I was not at Jerusalem; for in the thirty-second year of Artaxerxes king of Babylon I went to the king.” Arminian readers note that the problems arose during Nehemiah’s absence (cf. 5:14).

The length of his absence is not stated.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see how quickly faithfulness can slip without watchful leadership.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the account is honest about the community’s lapses.

verses.text: and I came to Jerusalem, and understood the evil that Eliashib had done for Tobiah, in preparing him a room in the courts of God’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah “understood the evil that Eliashib had done for Tobiah, in preparing him a room in the courts of God’s house.” Arminian readers note that Nehemiah names the act as evil.

The issue is the use of God’s house.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see zeal for the holiness of God’s house.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: what is set apart for God should not be turned to private advantage.

verses.text: It grieved me severely. Therefore I threw all Tobiah’s household stuff out of the room.
verses.arminianNotes:
“It grieved me severely. Therefore I threw all Tobiah’s household stuff out of the room.” Arminian readers note Nehemiah’s decisive action.

The text reports the act as part of his memoir.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see zeal for God’s house; some readers compare Jesus clearing the temple (John 2:13–17), as a reading.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the narrative reports Nehemiah’s response without presenting every detail as a model.

verses.text: Then I commanded, and they cleansed the rooms. I brought into them the vessels of God’s house, with the meal offerings and the frankincense again.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then I commanded, and they cleansed the rooms. I brought into them the vessels of God’s house, with the meal offerings and the frankincense again.” Arminian readers note that the rooms are restored to their purpose.

Cleansing is followed by restoration.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the proper use of God’s house reestablished.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: reform includes putting things back in their right place, not only removing what was wrong.

verses.text: I perceived that the portions of the Levites had not been given them, so that the Levites and the singers, who did the work, had each fled to his field.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah “perceived that the portions of the Levites had not been given them, so that the Levites and the singers, who did the work, had each fled to his field.” Arminian readers note that neglect of giving harmed those who served.

The pledge of 10:37–39 had not been kept.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see that worship suffers when God’s people do not support it (cf. Mal 3:8–10, often read alongside this passage).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: the Levites had to work their fields to live.

verses.text: Then I contended with the rulers, and said, “Why is God’s house forsaken?” I gathered them together, and set them in their place.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah contends with the rulers and asks, “Why is God’s house forsaken?” Arminian readers note that Nehemiah holds the leaders responsible.

The question recalls the pledge, “We will not forsake the house of our God” (10:39).
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see a call back to covenant commitments.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: Nehemiah gathers the Levites and sets them in their place again.

verses.text: Then all Judah brought the tithe of the grain, the new wine, and the oil to the treasuries.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Then all Judah brought the tithe of the grain, the new wine, and the oil to the treasuries.” Arminian readers note the people’s renewed response.

The reform is shared by the whole community.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see the people returning to their pledge.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: giving resumes, and the needs of those who serve are met.

verses.text: I made treasurers over the treasuries, Shelemiah the priest, and Zadok the scribe, and of the Levites, Pedaiah: and next to them was Hanan the son of Zaccur, the son of Mattaniah; for they were counted faithful, and their business was to distribute to their brothers.
verses.arminianNotes:
Nehemiah appoints treasurers, “for they were counted faithful, and their business was to distribute to their brothers.” Arminian readers note the importance of trustworthy stewards (cf. 1 Cor 4:2).

Priest, scribe, and Levite share the task.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers see faithfulness as the qualification for handling what belongs to God’s service.

Both traditions treat this as shared ground: careful stewardship protects both the gifts and those who depend on them.

verses.text: Remember me, my God, concerning this, and don’t wipe out my good deeds that I have done for the house of my God, and for its observances.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Remember me, my God, concerning this, and don’t wipe out my good deeds that I have done for the house of my God.” Arminian readers read the prayer as a servant asking God to receive his faithful work (cf. 5:19).

It is a prayer, not a claim of debt.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read it as an appeal to God’s faithfulness, and note that Nehemiah also asks God to spare him “according to the greatness of your loving kindness” (13:22).

Both traditions treat this as shared ground and do not read the prayer as earning salvation.
